  M -.-> L
blocks.caption: Left: the common-cause structure. Right: the cause-effect structure. A classical weight $p$ can select between them shot by shot; such mixtures are in neither pure hypothesis.

blocks.title: Correlations under each hypothesis
blocks.label: lem-l6-10-corr
blocks.md:
Under $H_{ce}$, with the Choi operator $J = \sum_{jk}|j\rangle\langle k| \otimes \mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|)$ of [L6-02](#lesson-l6-02),
$$c_i = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\,\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)] = \operatorname{Tr}\big[(\sigma_i^{T} \otimes \sigma_i)\,J/2\big].$$

With $A$ maximally mixed, $a = \pm 1$ each with probability $\tfrac12$ and the post-measurement state is $(I + a\sigma_i)/2$. So $\mathbb{E}[ab] = \sum_a \tfrac12\,a\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\,\mathcal{E}((I + a\sigma_i)/2)] = \tfrac14\sum_a (a\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(I)] + \operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)]) = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)]$. For the second form, $\operatorname{Tr}[(M \otimes N)J] = \sum_{jk}\langle k|M|j\rangle\operatorname{Tr}[N\mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|)] = \operatorname{Tr}[N\mathcal{E}(M^{T})]$; put $M = \sigma_i^{T}$, $N = \sigma_i$. $\square$

sections.heading: What each regime lets you do

blocks.md:
Which operations are available decides which distinctions are possible ([L6-04](#lesson-l6-04)). Two regimes are worth separating.

**Regime I: interventions on $A$.** If you can discard whatever arrives at $A$ and prepare a state of your choice there (a replacement intervention), the question becomes a signaling test. Under $H_{cc}$, $B$'s state is $\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$ whatever you prepare. Under $H_{ce}$, $B$'s state is $\mathcal{E}(\tau)$ for the prepared $\tau$.

blocks.title: Six preparations detect every non-constant channel
blocks.label: prop-l6-10-six
blocks.md: Let $\tau$ range over the six Pauli eigenstates $|0\rangle, |1\rangle, |\pm\rangle, |\pm i\rangle$ and let $B$ be measured in all three Pauli bases. If the statistics at $B$ do not depend on $\tau$, then $\mathcal{E}$ is a replacement channel $\mathcal{E}(\tau) = \operatorname{Tr}(\tau)\,\beta$. Conversely every replacement channel, and every common cause, gives $\tau$-independent statistics.

Pauli expectations determine a qubit state, so $\mathcal{E}(\tau) = \beta$ for all six $\tau$. By linearity $\mathcal{E}(Z) = \mathcal{E}(|0\rangle\langle 0|) - \mathcal{E}(|1\rangle\langle 1|) = 0$, and likewise $\mathcal{E}(X) = \mathcal{E}(Y) = 0$, while $\mathcal{E}(I) = 2\beta$. Hence $\mathcal{E}(M) = \operatorname{Tr}(M)\beta$ for every operator $M$. The converse is immediate. $\square$

So with interventions a non-constant channel is detectable, but a replacement channel is a direct-cause structure with no detectable influence: it is indistinguishable from no arrow at all. That is a faithfulness-type assumption that must be stated, not a fact quantum theory supplies. Interventions also say nothing about whether a common source is present in addition to the channel.

**Regime II: observation only.** If you cannot replace $A$, only measure it and let it continue, the measure-and-send protocol of Definition [](#def-l6-10-hyp) is what you have. Classically, passive observation of two variables cannot separate a common cause from a direct cause without further assumptions. With qubits, the three correlations carry structural information, as the next section proves. The rest of the lesson designs the Regime II experiment.

sections.heading: A statistic whose allowed ranges differ

blocks.title: Separating ranges
blocks.label: thm-l6-10-ranges
blocks.md:
Let $S = c_x + c_y + c_z$ in the measure-and-send protocol.

1. Under $H_{cc}$: $-3 \le S \le 1$. $S = 1$ exactly when $\rho_{AB}$ is supported on the triplet subspace, and $S = -3$ exactly for the singlet $|\Psi^-\rangle$.
2. Under $H_{ce}$: $-1 \le S \le 3$. $S = 3$ exactly for the identity channel.

So $S > 1$ is impossible for every common cause and $S < -1$ is impossible for every cause-effect channel.

*Common cause.* $S = \operatorname{Tr}[\rho_{AB}(XX + YY + ZZ)]$, and $XX + YY + ZZ = 2\,\mathrm{SWAP} - I$ (check it on $|00\rangle$, $|01\rangle$, $|10\rangle$, $|11\rangle$). $\mathrm{SWAP}$ has eigenvalue $+1$ on the three-dimensional triplet subspace and $-1$ on the singlet, so $XX + YY + ZZ$ has eigenvalues $1, 1, 1, -3$, and $S$ is a convex combination of them, with the stated equality cases.

*Cause-effect.* By Lemma [](#lem-l6-10-corr), and since $X^{T} = X$, $Y^{T} = -Y$, $Z^{T} = Z$ in the computational basis, $S = \operatorname{Tr}[(XX - YY + ZZ)\,J/2]$. Now $XX - YY + ZZ$ is the partial transpose (on the first factor) of $XX + YY + ZZ$, that is $2\,\mathrm{SWAP}^{T_A} - I = 2|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega| - I$ with $|\Omega\rangle = |00\rangle + |11\rangle$. Since $\langle\Omega|\Omega\rangle = 2$, its eigenvalues are $3, -1, -1, -1$. Because $\mathcal{E}$ is completely positive and trace preserving, $J/2$ is a density operator, so $-1 \le S \le 3$, with $S = 3$ iff $J/2 = |\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|/2$, the Choi state of the identity channel. $\square$

blocks.latex: XX + YY + ZZ = 2\,\mathrm{SWAP} - I, \qquad XX - YY + ZZ = 2|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega| - I
blocks.label: eq-l6-10-spectra

blocks.alt: A derivation that turns the common-cause value of S into a spectrum with largest eigenvalue 1, and the cause-effect value into a spectrum with smallest eigenvalue -1; then a number line from -3 to 3 with a blue common-cause interval, a red cause-effect interval, a gray overlap labeled inconclusive, and a dot that slides as the mixing weight grows.
blocks.caption: Equation [](#eq-l6-10-spectra) turns into two ranges on one number line. The mixture point $S = 3v(2p - 1)$ crosses from 'falsifies $H_{ce}$' through 'no verdict' to 'falsifies $H_{cc}$'.
blocks.describe: The statistic $S = c_x + c_y + c_z$ appears. The common-cause line $S_{cc} = \operatorname{Tr}[\rho_{AB}(XX + YY + ZZ)]$ transforms into $XX + YY + ZZ = 2\,\mathrm{SWAP} - I$ and then into eigenvalues $1, 1, 1, -3$, so $-3 \le S_{cc} \le 1$. The cause-effect line $S_{ce} = \operatorname{Tr}[(XX - YY + ZZ)J/2]$, with the note that $Y^{T} = -Y$ makes this the partial transpose, transforms into $XX - YY + ZZ = 2|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega| - I$ and eigenvalues $3, -1, -1, -1$, so $-1 \le S_{ce} \le 3$. A number line from $-3$ to $3$ shows the common-cause interval $[-3, 1]$ in blue, the cause-effect interval $[-1, 3]$ in red, and the overlap $[-1, 1]$ shaded as inconclusive. For the mixture model $S = 3v(2p - 1)$ with $v = 0.9$, a dot slides as $p$ goes from 0 to 1: at $p = 0$ it sits at $-2.70$ and falsifies $H_{ce}$; between $p \approx 0.31$ and $0.69$ there is no verdict; at $p = 0.75$, $S = 1.35$ and it falsifies $H_{cc}$.

blocks.title: The planned alternative: a mixture
blocks.label: ex-l6-10-mixture
blocks.md: Let each shot use a direct depolarized wire $\rho \mapsto v\rho + (1 - v)I/2$ with probability $p$, and a noisy singlet source $v|\Psi^-\rangle\langle\Psi^-| + (1 - v)I/4$ with probability $1 - p$. Both have $A$ maximally mixed, so the $A$ data cannot reveal the structure. The wire gives $c = v(1, 1, 1)$, the source gives $c = -v(1, 1, 1)$, so the mixture gives $S = 3v(2p - 1)$. With $v = 0.9$: $p = 0$ gives $-2.7$ (outside the cause-effect range), $p = 0.75$ gives $S = 1.35$ (outside the common-cause range), and every $p$ with $|2p - 1| \le 1/(3v)$, about $0.31 \le p \le 0.69$, lands in the overlap. A pure noisy wire ($p = 1$) falsifies $H_{cc}$ only if $3v > 1$, that is $v > 1/3$. Note the labeling: here $p$ is the weight of the direct wire, whereas in [L6-04](#lesson-l6-04) and in Ried et al. $p$ is the weight of the common cause.

blocks.title: What the overlap means
blocks.md: Every point of $[-1, 1]$ is reachable by both hypotheses, so a true value there gives no verdict at any sample size. In particular, every product state gives $|c_x| + |c_y| + |c_z| \le 1$ and so lies in the overlap: in this protocol, an unambiguous common-cause verdict needs entanglement, as Lab 11 shows. Not rejecting $H_{cc}$ is never evidence for $H_{cc}$ by itself.

sections.heading: How many shots: a bound that holds for every model

blocks.md: The estimate is $\hat S = \hat c_x + \hat c_y + \hat c_z$, each $\hat c_i$ the mean of $N$ products $ab \in \{-1, 1\}$. Because $H_{cc}$ is a set of models, an error bound computed for one convenient model (say, a normal approximation at the boundary) is not enough. A concentration inequality gives a bound that holds for every model at once.

blocks.title: Hoeffding's lemma
blocks.label: lem-l6-10-hlemma
blocks.md: [@hoeffding1963] If $Y \in [a, b]$ and $\mathbb{E}Y = 0$, then $\mathbb{E}\,e^{\lambda Y} \le e^{\lambda^2(b - a)^2/8}$ for every real $\lambda$.

By convexity, $e^{\lambda y} \le \frac{b - y}{b - a}e^{\lambda a} + \frac{y - a}{b - a}e^{\lambda b}$ on $[a, b]$. Taking expectations with $\mathbb{E}Y = 0$ gives $\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda Y} \le e^{L(h)}$ with $h = \lambda(b - a)$, $\pi = -a/(b - a) \in [0, 1]$ and $L(h) = -h\pi + \ln(1 - \pi + \pi e^{h})$. Then $L(0) = L'(0) = 0$ and $L''(h) = u(1 - u) \le \tfrac14$ with $u = \pi e^{h}/(1 - \pi + \pi e^{h})$, so Taylor's theorem gives $L(h) \le h^2/8$. $\square$

blocks.title: Hoeffding bound for the estimate of S
blocks.label: thm-l6-10-hoeffding
blocks.md:
If the $3N$ shots are independent, then for every model and every $t > 0$ [@hoeffding1963],
$$P(\hat S - S \ge t) \le e^{-N t^2/6}, \qquad P(\hat S - S \le -t) \le e^{-N t^2/6}.$$

$\hat S - S = \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^{3N}(Y_j - \mathbb{E}Y_j)$ with $Y_j \in [-1, 1]$. By Markov's inequality and independence, for $\lambda > 0$, $P(\sum_j (Y_j - \mathbb{E}Y_j) \ge Nt) \le e^{-\lambda N t}\prod_j \mathbb{E}e^{\lambda(Y_j - \mathbb{E}Y_j)} \le e^{-\lambda N t + 3N\lambda^2 \cdot 4/8}$ by the lemma (range 2). Minimizing over $\lambda$ at $\lambda = t/3$ gives $e^{-N t^2/6}$. The lower tail follows by applying this to $-Y_j$. $\square$

blocks.title: Valid tests and a sample size
blocks.label: prop-l6-10-size
blocks.md:
Let $t_N = \sqrt{6\ln(1/\alpha)/N}$. Reject $H_{cc}$ if $\hat S > 1 + t_N$ and reject $H_{ce}$ if $\hat S < -1 - t_N$. Then each true hypothesis is rejected with probability at most $\alpha$, for every model in it, and the chance of any false rejection is at most $2\alpha$. If the true $S \ge 1 + \Delta$, the test rejects $H_{cc}$ with probability at least $1 - \beta$ whenever
$$N \ge \frac{6\big(\sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)} + \sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)}\big)^2}{\Delta^2}.$$

Under $H_{cc}$, $S \le 1$ by Theorem [](#thm-l6-10-ranges), so $P(\hat S > 1 + t_N) \le P(\hat S - S > t_N) \le e^{-N t_N^2/6} = \alpha$; the other test is symmetric, and the union bound gives $2\alpha$. If $S \ge 1 + \Delta$ with $\Delta > t_N$, then $P(\hat S \le 1 + t_N) \le P(\hat S - S \le -(\Delta - t_N)) \le e^{-N(\Delta - t_N)^2/6}$, which is at most $\beta$ iff $\sqrt{N}\Delta \ge \sqrt{6\ln(1/\alpha)} + \sqrt{6\ln(1/\beta)}$. $\square$

**The numbers.** Take $\alpha = 0.025$ per test (at most $0.05$ in total), $\beta = 0.1$, and the planned alternative of Example [](#ex-l6-10-mixture) with $v = 0.9$, $p = 0.75$, so $S = 1.35$ and $\Delta = 0.35$. Then $6(\sqrt{\ln 40} + \sqrt{\ln 10})^2/0.35^2 \approx 578.96$, so $N = 579$ shots per setting, $1737$ in all, and $t_{579} = \sqrt{6\ln 40/579} \approx 0.196$. The pre-registered rule is: falsify $H_{cc}$ if $\hat S > 1.196$, falsify $H_{ce}$ if $\hat S < -1.196$.

blocks.caption: Exact sampling distributions of $\hat S$ at the boundary null ($S = 1$) and the planned alternative ($S = 1.35$), with the threshold $1 + t_N$, for $N = 30, 100, 300, 579$.

A dashed line marks the threshold $1 + t_N$. At $N = 30$ the curves overlap heavily, $t_N = 0.859$ and the power is $0.040$. At $N = 100$, $t_N = 0.470$ and the power is $0.220$. At $N = 300$, $t_N = 0.272$ and the power is $0.815$. At $N = 579$, $t_N = 0.196$ and the power is $0.992$. A closing note says that the Hoeffding guarantee holds for every common-cause model, not only the boundary one.

As $N$ sweeps, a red dot traces the exact binomial power for $S = 1.35$ and a violet dot traces the Hoeffding guarantee $1 - e^{-N(\Delta - t_N)^2/6}$, which stays at 0 until $t_N < \Delta$. A vertical line marks $N = 579$. The text reports the exact power $0.992$, the guarantee $\ge 0.9$, and the sample-size formula $N \ge 6(\sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)} + \sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)})^2/\Delta^2$.

Blue: exact type I error at the boundary null, far below $\alpha = 0.025$. The sawtooth comes from the discreteness of the binomial distribution.

blocks.title: Why not plan with the exact power?
blocks.md: For $S = 1.35$ the exact power first reaches $0.9$ at $N = 363$ and stays above it from $N = 370$, well below 579, and the exact type I error at the triplet state is about $0.0019$. The exact calculation, however, assumes a particular model in each hypothesis ($c$ along the diagonal). The Hoeffding bound assumes only independence and bounded outcomes, so it protects every model in the composite hypothesis. The price of that guarantee is about 60 percent more shots. Report which one you planned with.

sections.heading: Controls, the analysis plan, and what would falsify what

blocks.md: Theorem [](#thm-l6-10-ranges) relies on four assumptions, and each needs a control: trusted Pauli measurements on both qubits; a maximally mixed $A$ under $H_{ce}$; independent shots (no drift, no memory); and the identification of the recorded ports with the qubits $A$ and $B$ that the hypotheses describe.

blocks.title: A stuck detector looks like a perfect wire
blocks.md: If both detectors always report $+1$, every product $ab$ is $+1$ and $\hat S = 3$, the value of the identity channel. Symmetric, uncorrelated readout flips only shrink $|c_i|$ (each $c_i$ is multiplied by $(1 - 2e_A)(1 - 2e_B)$), which is conservative; biased or correlated readout errors are not. That is why the marginals are recorded and checked, not only the products.

blocks.title: Pre-registered analysis plan
blocks.label: alg-l6-10-plan
blocks.md:
1. **Fix in advance:** $\alpha = 0.025$ per test, $N = 579$ shots per setting, the thresholds $\pm 1.196$, and the order of settings (randomized and interleaved with control runs in blocks).
2. **Readout calibration:** prepare $|0\rangle, |1\rangle, |\pm\rangle, |\pm i\rangle$ on each qubit; estimate flip rates; stop if they are biased beyond a pre-set tolerance.
3. **Positive controls:** a known wire in place of the device (expect $\hat S$ near $3$ times the measured visibility) and a known entangled source (expect $\hat S$ near $-3$ times its visibility).
4. **Negative control:** a product source such as $|00\rangle$, which sits on the boundary $S = 1$; it must not be rejected more often than $\alpha$.
5. **Assumption check:** the $A$ marginals $\langle a\rangle_i$ must be zero within a Hoeffding margin; if not, $H_{ce}$ as defined is already falsified, and the ranges must be rederived for a non-mixed input.
6. **Main run:** compute $\hat c_x, \hat c_y, \hat c_z$ and $\hat S$; apply the rule; report $\hat S$ with its margin $t_N$ whatever the verdict.
7. **Replication:** confirm any verdict on an independent run before reporting it as established.

| Result | Falsifies | Does not show |
|---|---|---|
| $\hat S > 1 + t_N$ | every common-cause model in the protocol | that the channel is the identity, or that no source is present at all |
| $\hat S < -1 - t_N$ | every cause-effect model with mixed input | which entangled source produced it |
| $\lvert\hat S\rvert \le 1 + t_N$ | nothing | that either hypothesis is true; the design cannot decide |
| both thresholds crossed in separate runs, or a control fails | the assumptions of the design | anything about the causal structure until the failure is explained |

blocks.caption: Seeded simulated experiments for each mixing weight $p$ (with $v = 0.9$). Move the slider to change the shots per setting. Red points falsify the common cause, blue points falsify the cause-effect channel, gray points give no verdict; the gray band is the overlap $[-1, 1]$.
blocks.describe: The horizontal axis is the mixing weight $p$ of the direct channel from 0 to 1; the vertical axis is $S$ from $-3.6$ to $3.6$. A line shows the true $S = 3v(2p - 1)$. For each $p$ in steps of $0.05$ a point shows a simulated $\hat S$ with error bar $\pm t_N$, colored by the verdict. Dashed lines at $\pm(1 + t_N)$ mark the rejection thresholds, and a shaded band marks $[-1, 1]$. With $N = 30$ the thresholds sit at about $\pm 1.86$ and few points are decisive; with $N = 579$ they sit at $\pm 1.196$; with $N = 3000$ they approach $\pm 1$, but points with true $S$ inside the band never become decisive.

sections.heading: Simulate the experiment

blocks.explain: A qubit-level simulation with seeded shots. Each shot first draws the structure (direct wire with probability $p$, noisy singlet source otherwise), then samples outcomes from the Born rule for the chosen Pauli pair. The run uses the planned $N = 579$ and applies the pre-registered rule and the $A$-marginal control.
blocks.source:
import math
import numpy as np
from qcai import science as s

PAULI = {"x": s.X, "y": s.Y, "z": s.Z}
KEYS_A = np.array([1, 1, -1, -1]); KEYS_B = np.array([1, -1, 1, -1])     # outcome pairs (a, b)
proj_pm = lambda P, a: (s.I2 + a * P) / 2

def table_common(rho, P):
    """Joint outcome probabilities when sigma_i is measured on both halves of a shared state."""
    return np.array([np.real(np.trace(rho @ np.kron(proj_pm(P, a), proj_pm(P, b)))) for a, b in zip(KEYS_A, KEYS_B)])

def table_channel(kraus, P):
    """A maximally mixed, measured (eigenstate kept), sent through the channel, then measured."""
    return np.array([0.5 * np.real(np.trace(proj_pm(P, b) @ s.apply_kraus(proj_pm(P, a), kraus)))
                     for a, b in zip(KEYS_A, KEYS_B)])

V, P_MIX = 0.9, 0.75
rho_cc = V * s.dm(s.bell_state("psi-")) + (1 - V) * np.eye(4) / 4      # noisy singlet source
kraus_ce = s.depolarizing_kraus(1 - V)                                  # rho -> V rho + (1 - V) I/2

# exact correlations of the two pure structures and of the mixture
for name, tab in (("common cause", table_common), ("cause-effect", table_channel)):
    arg = rho_cc if tab is table_common else kraus_ce
    c = [float(KEYS_A * KEYS_B @ tab(arg, P)) for P in PAULI.values()]
    print(f"{name:13s} c = {np.round(c, 4)}  S = {sum(c):+.3f}")
S_mix = 3 * V * (2 * P_MIX - 1)
print(f"mixture p = {P_MIX}: S = 3v(2p - 1) = {S_mix:.3f}")

def run_experiment(p_mix, n, rng):
    """n shots per Pauli setting; each shot first draws the structure (direct channel with prob p_mix)."""
    c_hat, a_mean = {}, {}
    for k, P in PAULI.items():
        tabs = (table_common(rho_cc, P), table_channel(kraus_ce, P))
        direct = rng.random(n) < p_mix
        idx = np.where(direct, rng.choice(4, size=n, p=tabs[1]), rng.choice(4, size=n, p=tabs[0]))
        c_hat[k] = float(np.mean(KEYS_A[idx] * KEYS_B[idx]))
        a_mean[k] = float(np.mean(KEYS_A[idx]))
    return c_hat, a_mean

ALPHA, BETA, DELTA = 0.025, 0.10, S_mix - 1
N = math.ceil(6 * (math.sqrt(math.log(1 / ALPHA)) + math.sqrt(math.log(1 / BETA))) ** 2 / DELTA ** 2)
t_N = math.sqrt(6 * math.log(1 / ALPHA) / N)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
c_hat, a_mean = run_experiment(P_MIX, N, rng)
S_hat = sum(c_hat.values())
print(f"\nplanned N = {N} per setting ({3 * N} shots), t_N = {t_N:.3f}")
print("estimates", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in c_hat.items()}, f" S_hat = {S_hat:.3f}")
verdict = ("falsifies common cause" if S_hat > 1 + t_N else
           "falsifies cause-effect" if S_hat < -1 - t_N else "no verdict")
print("decision:", verdict)
m = math.sqrt(2 * math.log(2 * 3 / 0.01) / N)            # A-marginal control, family-wise 0.01
print("A marginals", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in a_mean.items()}, f" control margin {m:.3f}:",
      "pass" if all(abs(v) <= m for v in a_mean.values()) else "FAIL")

blocks.explain: The design checks: exact binomial power and the Hoeffding guarantee at $N = 579$, the exact type I error at two boundary null models, a simulated false-rejection rate, the two spectra and a random search over states and channels, and the Regime I signaling statistic $D = P(b = 0 \mid |0\rangle) - P(b = 0 \mid |1\rangle)$, which equals $pv$ in the mixture model and $0$ for every common cause.
blocks.source:
# exact power (binomial) and the Hoeffding guarantee; the type I error at two boundary null models
def binom_pmf(n, q):
    k = np.arange(n + 1)
    logc = np.array([math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(i + 1) - math.lgamma(n - i + 1) for i in k])
    return np.exp(logc + k * math.log(q) + (n - k) * math.log1p(-q))

thr = lambda n: math.floor(n * (4 + math.sqrt(6 * math.log(1 / ALPHA) / n)) / 2)
power = lambda S, n: float(binom_pmf(3 * n, (1 + S / 3) / 2)[thr(n) + 1:].sum())   # c = (S/3)(1, 1, 1)
print(f"exact power at N = {N}: {power(S_mix, N):.3f};  Hoeffding guarantee "
      f"{1 - math.exp(-N * (DELTA - t_N) ** 2 / 6):.3f}")
print(f"exact type I at the triplet state (c = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)): {power(1.0, N):.4f}")
pmf = np.convolve(binom_pmf(N, 0.5), binom_pmf(N, 0.5))
print(f"exact type I at |00> (c = (0, 0, 1)): {pmf[np.arange(pmf.size) + N > thr(N)].sum():.4f}")

# coverage of the Hoeffding test by simulation at the boundary null, N = 100
g = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 100
K = g.binomial(n, (1 + 1 / 3) / 2, size=(20000, 3)).sum(axis=1)
S_rep = (2 * K - 3 * n) / n
print(f"false rejections in 20000 simulated boundary experiments: {np.mean(S_rep > 1 + math.sqrt(6 * math.log(40) / n)):.4f}"
      f" (guaranteed <= {ALPHA})")

# the witness spectra, and random states and channels
XX, YY, ZZ = (np.kron(P, P) for P in (s.X, s.Y, s.Z))
print("eig(XX+YY+ZZ) =", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(XX + YY + ZZ), 6), " eig(XX-YY+ZZ) =", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(XX - YY + ZZ), 6))
SWAP = np.eye(4)[[0, 2, 1, 3]]
pt = lambda M: M.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2).transpose(2, 1, 0, 3).reshape(4, 4)   # transpose on the first factor
omega = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1.0])
assert np.allclose(XX + YY + ZZ, 2 * SWAP - np.eye(4)) and np.allclose(pt(SWAP), np.outer(omega, omega))
worst_cc, worst_ce = -9.0, 9.0
for _ in range(300):
    G = g.normal(size=(4, 4)) + 1j * g.normal(size=(4, 4)); rho = G @ G.conj().T; rho /= np.trace(rho)
    worst_cc = max(worst_cc, float(np.real(np.trace(rho @ (XX + YY + ZZ)))))
    Q = np.linalg.qr(g.normal(size=(6, 6)) + 1j * g.normal(size=(6, 6)))[0][:, :2].reshape(2, 3, 2)
    kr = [Q[:, k, :] for k in range(3)]
    worst_ce = min(worst_ce, sum(float(KEYS_A * KEYS_B @ table_channel(kr, P)) for P in PAULI.values()))
print(f"300 random states: max S = {worst_cc:.3f} (<= 1);  300 random channels: min S = {worst_ce:.3f} (>= -1)")

# intervention regime: replace A by |0> or |1>, measure Z on B
n_int = 200
def b_zero_prob(prep):
    direct = s.apply_kraus(s.dm(prep), kraus_ce)[0, 0].real
    return P_MIX * direct + (1 - P_MIX) * 0.5                 # common-cause branch: B stays I/2
p0, p1 = b_zero_prob(s.KET0), b_zero_prob(s.KET1)
D_hat = g.binomial(n_int, p0) / n_int - g.binomial(n_int, p1) / n_int
print(f"\nintervention: D = {p0 - p1:.3f} (= p v), D_hat = {D_hat:.3f}, one-sided margin {math.sqrt(math.log(1 / ALPHA) / n_int):.3f}")

blocks.title: Simulations are not experiments
blocks.md: The simulation checks that the analysis behaves as designed when its assumptions hold. It cannot check the assumptions: real readout bias, drift, leakage out of the qubit subspace, or a structure outside both hypotheses can all produce a crossing of a threshold. Those are what the controls in Algorithm [](#alg-l6-10-plan) are for.

worked_example.title: Sizing a run for a weaker alternative
worked_example.problem: A team expects a pure noisy wire with visibility $v = 0.45$ and wants to falsify $H_{cc}$ with $\alpha = 0.025$ and power at least $0.9$ under the Hoeffding guarantee. Find $S$, $\Delta$, the required $N$ per setting, the threshold, and decide whether a result $\hat S = 1.21$ at that $N$ falsifies $H_{cc}$.
steps: A pure wire is $p = 1$ in Example [](#ex-l6-10-mixture), so $S = 3v = 1.35$ and $\Delta = S - 1 = 0.35$, the same gap as the planned mixture.
Threshold: $t_{579} = \sqrt{6 \cdot 3.6889/579} \approx 0.196$, so reject $H_{cc}$ if $\hat S > 1.196$.
Decision: $1.21 > 1.196$, so $H_{cc}$ is rejected at level $0.025$. The margin is small; the plan's replication step applies before the verdict is reported as established.
worked_example.result: $N = 579$ per setting, threshold $1.196$; $\hat S = 1.21$ falsifies every common-cause model in the protocol at level $0.025$, subject to replication and to the controls passing.

exercises.prompt: Compute $S$ in the protocol for (a) the state $|\Phi^+\rangle$ as a common cause, (b) the identity channel, (c) the bit-flip channel $\rho \mapsto X\rho X$. Which hypotheses can each be falsified by, with enough shots?
exercises.solution: (a) $c = (1, -1, 1)$, $S = 1$: inside the overlap, no verdict at any $N$. (b) $c = (1, 1, 1)$, $S = 3$: outside $[-3, 1]$, so it can falsify $H_{cc}$. (c) $c_i = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i X\sigma_i X] = (1, -1, -1)$, $S = -1$: on the boundary of the cause-effect range, inside the overlap, no verdict.

exercises.prompt: With $\alpha = 0.025$, what is the threshold $1 + t_N$ for $N = 300$ shots per setting, and what is the smallest $\Delta$ for which the Hoeffding guarantee gives power $0.9$ at that $N$?
Show that every product state $\rho_A \otimes \rho_B$ gives $|S| \le 1$, so that in this protocol only entangled sources can falsify $H_{ce}$.
exercises.solution: For a product state $c_i = r_i s_i$ with Bloch vectors $\vec r, \vec s$ of length at most 1. Then $|S| \le \sum_i |r_i||s_i| \le |\vec r||\vec s| \le 1$ by Cauchy-Schwarz. Mixtures of product states (separable states) are convex combinations, so $|S| \le 1$ too, and $S < -1$ requires entanglement.

exercises.prompt: Readout on each qubit flips the outcome with probability $e$, independently and symmetrically. Show that every $c_i$ is multiplied by $(1 - 2e)^2$, and find the largest $e$ for which the pure identity channel can still falsify $H_{cc}$ with enough shots.
exercises.solution: A symmetric flip multiplies each outcome by an independent $\pm 1$ with mean $1 - 2e$, so $\mathbb{E}[ab]$ is multiplied by $(1 - 2e)^2$. The identity channel then gives $S = 3(1 - 2e)^2$, which exceeds 1 iff $(1 - 2e)^2 > 1/3$, i.e. $e < (1 - 1/\sqrt3)/2 \approx 0.211$.

exercises.prompt: Under $H_{ce}$, suppose $A$ is not maximally mixed but has Bloch vector $\vec r$. Show that $c_i = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)] + \tfrac12 r_i\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(I)]$. Then take $A$ in $|0\rangle$ and the channel $\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{Z} \circ \mathcal{D}_\gamma$, where $\mathcal{D}_\gamma$ is amplitude damping toward $|1\rangle$ ($|0\rangle\langle 0| \mapsto (1 - \gamma)|0\rangle\langle 0| + \gamma|1\rangle\langle 1|$, $|1\rangle\langle 1| \mapsto |1\rangle\langle 1|$, $|0\rangle\langle 1| \mapsto \sqrt{1 - \gamma}\,|0\rangle\langle 1|$) and $\mathcal{Z}(\rho) = Z\rho Z$. Compute $S(\gamma)$ and its minimum. What does this say about the marginal check?
exercises.solution: Outcome $a$ has probability $(1 + a r_i)/2$ and leaves $(I + a\sigma_i)/2$, so $\mathbb{E}[ab] = \sum_a \frac{1 + a r_i}{2}\cdot a\cdot\tfrac12\big(\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(I)] + a\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)]\big) = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)] + \tfrac12 r_i\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma_i\mathcal{E}(I)]$. For the given channel, $\mathcal{E}(X) = -\sqrt{1 - \gamma}\,X$, $\mathcal{E}(Y) = -\sqrt{1 - \gamma}\,Y$, $\mathcal{E}(Z) = (1 - \gamma)Z$ and $\mathcal{E}(I) = I - \gamma Z$. With $\vec r = (0, 0, 1)$: $c_x = c_y = -\sqrt{1 - \gamma}$ and $c_z = (1 - \gamma) - \gamma$, so $S(\gamma) = 1 - 2\gamma - 2\sqrt{1 - \gamma}$. With $u = \sqrt{1 - \gamma}$, $S = 2u^2 - 2u - 1$, minimized at $u = \tfrac12$ ($\gamma = \tfrac34$) with $S = -1.5 < -1$. So a cause-effect structure with a biased input would be wrongly reported as falsifying $H_{ce}$. The bound $S \ge -1$ was proved only for a maximally mixed input; here $\langle a\rangle_z = 1$, which the marginal check in the plan detects at once.

exercises.prompt: Design the Regime I (intervention) version: with replacement preparations $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ at $A$, $n$ shots each, and a $Z$ measurement at $B$, give a level-$\alpha$ test of $H_{cc}$ based on $\hat D = \hat P(b = 0 \mid |0\rangle) - \hat P(b = 0 \mid |1\rangle)$, its sample size for the mixture model with $v = 0.9$, $p = 0.75$, and one cause-effect channel it cannot detect.
exercises.solution: Under $H_{cc}$, $D = 0$ for every model. $\hat D$ is a sum of $2n$ independent terms each in a range of length $1/n$, so Hoeffding gives $P(\hat D - D \ge t) \le e^{-2t^2/(2n \cdot n^{-2})} = e^{-n t^2}$. Reject $H_{cc}$ if $\hat D > \sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)/n}$. In the mixture model $D = pv = 0.675$; power $1 - \beta$ is guaranteed when $\sqrt{n}\,D \ge \sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)} + \sqrt{\ln(1/\beta)}$, i.e. $n \ge (1.9206 + 1.5174)^2/0.675^2 \approx 25.9$, so $n = 26$ per preparation. It cannot detect a channel that ignores the $Z$ basis, such as measure-$X$-and-prepare-$Z$, $\mathcal{E}(\tau) = \langle +|\tau|+\rangle|0\rangle\langle 0| + \langle -|\tau|-\rangle|1\rangle\langle 1|$, which sends both $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ to $I/2$; Proposition [](#prop-l6-10-six) says all six preparations and three bases are needed to catch every non-constant channel.

check.question: In the measure-and-send protocol, the estimate is $\hat S = 0.6 \pm 0.05$ with a very large $N$. What should be reported?
options: The direct channel is confirmed because $S > -1$
The common cause is confirmed because $S < 1$
check.explanation: $0.6$ lies in the overlap $[-1, 1]$ of the two ranges, so no model in either hypothesis is excluded. More shots cannot change that.

check.question: Why is the Hoeffding bound used for planning instead of a normal approximation at one boundary model?
options: It removes the need for controls
It bounds the error for every model in the composite hypothesis
It is exact for binomial data
check.explanation: A hypothesis such as 'some two-qubit state' contains infinitely many models. Hoeffding uses only independence and bounded outcomes, so the level-$\alpha$ guarantee holds for all of them; the price is more shots than an exact calculation for one model.

check.question: Both detectors are stuck and always report $+1$. What does the analysis report?
options: Nothing, because the products are not recorded
$\hat S = 3$, a spurious falsification of the common cause unless the marginal and readout controls catch it
$\hat S = -3$, a falsification of the direct channel
check.explanation: Every product $ab$ is $+1$, so each $\hat c_i = 1$ and $\hat S = 3$. The marginals $\langle a\rangle = \langle b\rangle = 1$ fail the assumption check, which is why the plan records them.

check.question: Under the Choi convention $J = \sum_{jk}|j\rangle\langle k| \otimes \mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|)$, which expression gives $\operatorname{Tr}[N\,\mathcal{E}(M)]$?
check.explanation: $\operatorname{Tr}[(M' \otimes N)J] = \operatorname{Tr}[N\mathcal{E}(M'^{T})]$, so $M' = M^{T}$. Forgetting the transpose flips the sign of $c_y$ and swaps the two ranges of Theorem [](#thm-l6-10-ranges).

misconceptions.claim: "If the data do not reject the common cause, the common cause is supported."
misconceptions.correction: Values in $[-1, 1]$ are allowed by both hypotheses. Failing to reject is a non-result under this design and must be reported as one.

misconceptions.claim: "With enough shots any two causal hypotheses can be told apart."
misconceptions.correction: Shots shrink the margin $t_N$ but cannot move the true $S$ out of the overlap. Separation needs a statistic whose allowed ranges differ at the true model, which is a property of the design.

misconceptions.claim: "Rejecting both pure hypotheses is a contradiction, so the experiment failed."
misconceptions.correction: It cannot happen within one run (the two rejection regions are disjoint), but separate runs or failed controls can point outside both pure hypotheses: to a mixture of structures, to a structure with both a source and a channel, or to broken assumptions. Each is a substantive result once the controls are checked.

misconceptions.claim: "A significant result means the channel is the identity."
misconceptions.correction: Rejecting $H_{cc}$ excludes every common-cause model. It says nothing about which channel or mixture produced the data, and it does not exclude a source acting alongside a channel.

lessons.connect: Level 7 returns to identifiability and estimation for larger quantum causal models, where full process tomography and causal discovery algorithms replace a single witness [@giarmatzi; @costa]. Entropic constraints are another way to separate causal structures with latent systems [@chaves], and the pseudo-density-matrix approach gives an observational scheme that distinguishes more structures for two qubits measured at two times [@hypothesis].
lessons.caution: The design assumes trusted Pauli measurements, independent shots, a maximally mixed qubit $A$ under the cause-effect hypothesis, and the two pure structures as the hypotheses. Mixtures of structures, a source and a channel acting together, coherent superpositions of structures, and systems larger than qubits are outside both hypotheses and are not tested. Conventions: Choi operator $J = \sum_{jk}|j\rangle\langle k| \otimes \mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|)$ as in `qcai.science.choi`, transpose in the computational basis (so $Y^{T} = -Y$), outcomes $\pm 1$, natural logarithms. The stated level of the cause-effect test holds only for an exactly mixed input: by the biased-input formula of the fifth exercise, a bias $\vec r$ can loosen the bound $S \ge -1$, so passing the marginal check is necessary for using that test but does not correct for a small residual bias. The simulations check the analysis, not the physics, and none of this is a claim of quantum advantage for causal inference.

instructor.why: Students meet quantum causal models as theory; this lesson makes them do what an experimental collaborator must: state hypotheses as sets, find what they forbid, size a run with a guarantee that survives composite nulls, and write down what each result means [@ried2015; @costa; @barrett].
teaching_notes: Start by asking students to propose a statistic before showing the theorem; many propose $c_z$ alone and can be shown that $c_z = 1$ is allowed by both hypotheses.
Derive $XX + YY + ZZ = 2\,\mathrm{SWAP} - I$ on the board from the action on the computational basis; the partial-transpose step then needs only $Y^{T} = -Y$.
Use the interactive at $N = 30$ and $N = 3000$ to separate sampling uncertainty from structural non-identifiability; the points inside the gray band never become decisive.
Have groups write the pre-registered plan before running the code, then compare their thresholds and controls with Algorithm [](#alg-l6-10-plan).
instructor.assessment: The core exercises test the ranges and the threshold arithmetic; the stretch exercises test the role of entanglement and of readout error; the challenge exercises test whether students can redo the design for a biased input and for the intervention regime.
instructor.extend: Extend the hypotheses to probabilistic mixtures of the two structures and ask which values of $c$ certify a nonzero direct-cause weight; compare with the experiment on coherent mixtures [@maclean]. For full structure learning from process data, see the algorithm of Giarmatzi and Costa [@giarmatzi].

further.note: The two-qubit common-cause versus cause-effect question with the measure-and-send protocol, and a photonic experiment.
An experiment on coherent mixtures of common-cause and cause-effect relations.
An observational scheme based on space-time pseudo-density matrices that distinguishes five causal structures.

unit.big_question: What does it mean for one quantum system to cause another, and which causal claims can quantum experiments test?
unit.summary: Learners start from Bell's theorem read as a statement about one causal graph, then build the tools that quantum causal models need: Choi operators with explicit conventions, process operators, and a Markov condition made of commuting channel operators. They learn which classical results survive (Markovianity is equivalent to an underlying unitary circuit, and d-separation stays sound and complete for a quantum notion of independence) and which do not (screening off by a classical common cause, reading absent arrows off zero correlations). The second half covers interventions at quantum nodes, causal discovery and its limits, Bell and causal inequalities, process matrices without a fixed order, the quantum switch, and counterfactual questions, and ends with the design of a quantum causal experiment with stated assumptions.
unit.for_whom: Graduate students and advanced undergraduates who have completed Levels 4 and 5 or have equivalent background: structural causal models and d-separation, density operators, channels in Kraus form, and the CHSH test. It suits a graduate seminar, a reading course, or independent study before research in quantum foundations, quantum information or causal inference.
unit.prerequisites: Comfort with linear algebra over complex numbers (tensor products, partial traces, spectral decompositions), the density-operator and channel formalism of Level 5, and the causal graphs and identification ideas of Level 4.

time.pace: One lesson a week with a problem session fits a semester alongside the project. Each lesson splits into a reading and animation session, a proof and computation session, and an exercise session.

session_flow: Before the session: watch the animations and read the definitions; write down one claim you doubt.
Open with the motivating puzzle and the check question that reviews an earlier lesson.
Work through the theorems and proofs at the board; state every convention (factor order, normalization, transposes).
Run the code cells, change one parameter, and predict the output before running it again.
Solve the core and stretch exercises in pairs; attempt one challenge exercise alone.
Close with the caution section: what the lesson does not show and which assumptions it used.

outcomes.text: I can derive the CHSH bound from the Bell causal graph, name the assumption behind each step, and explain how a quantum common cause exceeds it without signalling.
I can build Choi operators in a stated convention, test complete positivity and trace preservation, and compose channels with the link product.
I can write the process operator of a quantum causal model, check the commutation conditions, and say which d-separation statements hold and in which sense.
I can model an intervention at a quantum node as an instrument and compute its effect on downstream predictions.
I can explain what interventional and observational data can and cannot reveal about quantum causal structure.
I can state the validity conditions of a process matrix and distinguish Bell inequalities from causal inequalities.
I can describe the quantum switch as a process and evaluate a claimed advantage with explicit resource accounting.
I can design a quantum causal experiment that states its hypotheses, conventions, assumptions and the data that would refute it.

unit.evidence: Each lesson has three or four check questions (one reviews an earlier lesson) and graded exercises at core, stretch and challenge level with complete solutions. Proof exercises are assessed for correct use of conventions. The project is a written and computational report judged with a four-part rubric.
materials: Python 3 with numpy, scipy, matplotlib, plotly and networkx (the course package qcai provides the shared helpers)
The course labs on Bell tests, noise channels and quantum causal inference (Colab or Binder)
A notebook for proofs and conventions; a shared document for the project report
Access to the cited papers (all have open preprints)

project.title: A quantum causal model, end to end
project.summary: Over four sessions, the learner chooses a small quantum causal hypothesis, writes it as a quantum causal model in a stated convention, verifies it numerically, compares it with a rival hypothesis, and proposes an experiment with explicit assumptions.
questions: Can a fixed set of local measurements distinguish a shared entangled state from a channel between two qubits, and where do the two hypotheses predict the same data?
A qubit passes through two noisy steps. When does the process factorize as a chain, and what signature would reveal an environment that keeps a memory between the steps?
In a three-node network with one shared parent, which conditional independences does the graph force, and which interventions would expose a hidden influence that the data alone conceal?
steps: State the question, the competing causal hypotheses as DAGs, and the formalism (Allen et al. or Barrett et al., or another with a reason).
Fix and write down the conventions: Choi factor order, normalization, and where transposes enter.
Build the process operators for each hypothesis and verify normalization, positivity and the Markov commutation conditions in code.
Compute predictions for at least two choices of interventions, including one that separates the hypotheses if any does.
Check the graph-implied independences with d-separation and say in which sense (quantum node, observed classical node, or setting and outcome) each holds.
Write the report: claim, model, conventions, computations, assumptions (including faithfulness), what would refute the claim, and what the simulation does not show.

rubric.start: I drew a graph for my scenario.
rubric.got: I wrote the process operators for each hypothesis in a stated convention.
rubric.explain: I can justify the formalism and explain how the same experiment would be drawn in another one.

rubric.start: I ran code that produces numbers.
rubric.got: My code checks normalization, positivity and commutation and matches direct simulation.
rubric.explain: I can show which check would fail for a wrong convention and why.

rubric.got: I derived the independences the graph forces and the interventions that separate the hypotheses.
rubric.explain: I can say which conclusions need faithfulness and give an example where it fails.

rubric.got: I stated assumptions, conventions and what would refute the claim.
rubric.explain: I can separate what the simulation shows from what an experiment would need, including resources and noise.

udl: Every animation has a full text description, and every interactive figure has a written summary of what it shows.
Results are presented three ways where possible: a picture, a theorem with proof, and code that checks it numerically.
Exercises come at three levels; learners may answer proof questions with a numerical counterexample search first and a proof second.
Learners can present the project as a written report, a notebook, or a short talk with slides.

readings.note: Quantum common causes and the quantum Reichenbach principle; the foundation for L6-01 and L6-03.
Quantum causal models from unitary circuits, quantum d-separation and do-calculus rules.
Rigorous treatment of channels and the Choi representation.
Quantum networks and combs built with the link product.
A process-based formulation of quantum causal modelling.
Process matrices and correlations with no definite causal order.
A graph-separation rule for quantum networks without the common-cause factorization.
An experiment showing a quantum advantage in inferring causal structure.

unit.approach: The unit was planned backward from its outcomes [@ubd_whitepaper], and each lesson moves from a puzzle and an animation, to definitions and theorems with proofs, to computation and practice [@merrill2002], with a review question in every check [@dunlosky2013]. Animations are made with Manim Community Edition [@manim_ce] from the same numbers as the text. The causal content follows the quantum causal model frameworks of Allen et al. and Barrett, Lorenz and Oreshkov [@allen; @barrett], compared with process-based and network approaches [@costa; @chiribella; @pienaar; @hlp2014], and the channel calculus follows Watrous [@watrous]. Conventions are stated in every lesson, because results in this field change with factor orders and transposes.
